The report points readers to financial and reserves data; notes its extensive proprietary technology and 8,000-plus patents, none individually essential to segment profitability; and outlines long-term talent development, workforce diversity, benefits, and employee counts. It also flags regulatory and other business risks and identifies where further information appears. Finally, it explains website access to SEC filings and governance materials, clarifying website content is not incorporated into the report, and notes the SEC’s filings database.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Supply and Demand
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s results and financial condition face risks from commodity price and margin swings, supply and demand, and the uncertain commercial viability of lower-emission and new businesses. Demand may be affected by economic downturns, geopolitical and trade disruptions, financial-market stress, public-health events, technology, weather, alternative energy, consumer preferences, AI data-center growth, and income levels. Supply risks include capacity growth, production quotas, policy and funding constraints, conflict, disasters, logistics, new resources and shipping routes, and technological change. Interest rates, inflation, currency and U.S.-dollar trends, regional markets, and related hedging or trading losses also pose risks.

nodes.title: Government and Political Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil faces political and regulatory risks that may harm results: limits on resource access, production, foreign investment, trade, and business dealings; sanctions that may advantage competitors; and weak or shifting legal systems that undermine compliance and contract enforcement. Legal and policy changes may raise taxes, royalties, costs, or restrictions; delay permits, incentives, transport, or markets; impose disclosure and technology standards; or enable contract changes and expropriation. Litigation, investigations, enforcement, and inadequate remedies may cause liability and damages. Civil unrest, conflict, sabotage, piracy, terrorism, cyberattacks, security policies, strikes, and protests may increase costs or disrupt operations.

nodes.title: Climate Change and Energy Transition
nodes.summary: The text outlines climate-transition risks and opportunities: net-zero goals rely on uncertain scenarios, supportive policies, technology, and timely investment decisions; ExxonMobil aims for net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions from operated assets but notes societal progress is lagging. Emissions policies and pressure on oil-and-gas financing may raise costs, delay projects, reduce hydrocarbon demand, and affect returns. Scaling lower-emission technologies—including CCS, hydrogen, lower-emission fuels, lithium, and other solutions—depends on successful research and partnerships. Commercial deployment and returns require stable government support and markets; policy delays or restricting supply without reducing demand may cause volatility, inflation, shortages, and economic harm.

nodes.title: Operational and Other Factors
nodes.summary: Business results depend on managing controllable factors and, for non-operated projects, co-venturers. Risks include exploration and development success; complex project execution, contracts, costs, technical issues, markets, incentives, operators, and portfolio acquisitions or divestments and residual liabilities; operational efficiency, technology, workforce, and integration; research, development, and adoption of technologies including AI and emissions-reduction tools; safety, environmental protection, controls, and enterprise risk management; cybersecurity threats, including through third parties; severe weather, disasters, and preparedness; limited insurance availability and affordability; competition from private and state-owned firms, alternative energy, and new entrants; and reputational harm. Forward-looking plans and estimates may differ materially from actual outcomes because of these and other risks.

ExxonMobil’s results and financial condition face risks from volatile commodity prices, margins, supply and demand, economic and market conditions, and uncertain new-business viability. Political, regulatory, legal, geopolitical, security, and social developments may restrict access or trade, raise costs, disrupt operations, or create liabilities. Climate policies, transition goals, technology, investment, and market support affect hydrocarbon demand and lower-emission business prospects. Operational risks include project execution, exploration, technology, workforce, safety, environmental controls, cybersecurity, disasters, insurance, competition, and reputation; actual outcomes may differ materially from forward-looking plans.

nodes.title: ITEM 1C. CYBERSECURITY
nodes.summary: The Corporation integrates cybersecurity into enterprise risk management, with annual Audit Committee review. Its IT Vice President and experienced IT/OT operations managers oversee daily prevention, detection, investigation, and response. Management reports on strategy, metrics, testing, preparedness, and threats. The program uses layered controls, NIST guidance, incident-response procedures, annual training, drills, threat sharing, and independent expert testing. Third-party reviews are risk-based. No known cyber risks have materially affected or are likely to materially affect the Corporation, but protections cannot eliminate all risks; related exposures are discussed in the report’s Risk Factors.

title: OVERVIEW

nodes.title: OVERVIEW (intro)
nodes.summary: Management is responsible for ExxonMobil’s financial reporting, which reflects its integrated operations across oil and gas, energy and chemical products, specialty products, and emerging lower-emission businesses. Reportable segments are Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, and Specialty Products, with voluntary geographic disclosures. The company is organized into Upstream, Product Solutions, and Low Carbon Solutions, supported by centralized service groups; Low Carbon Solutions is reported in Corporate and Financing as it develops. Its resources, finances, technology, and integrated model support investment in reliable, affordable, lower-emission energy and help moderate commodity-price risk. Annual Outlook and Corporate Plan processes set economic assumptions and operating and capital objectives, including prices, margins, volumes, costs, emissions pricing, and exchange rates. Investments are assessed across market conditions, based on long-term fundamentals and competitiveness, then reappraised so lessons inform future projects.

nodes.title: Long-Term Business Outlook
key_items: Developing countries projected to drive energy demand growth
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s Outlook projects global energy supply and demand through 2050, informing planning, investment, and research while drawing on multiple scenarios, including IPCC and IEA pathways. Because policies, markets, and technologies are uncertain, the company monitors transition signposts and adjusts future Outlooks. Population and economic growth are projected to raise global energy demand by over 10%, driven by developing countries, while developed-country use falls over 10%; efficiency lowers energy and emissions per unit of output. Electricity demand rises over 70%, mostly in developing countries. Coal’s generation share falls from about 35% to 15%; gas, nuclear, and renewables supply electricity growth, with wind and solar rising nearly 400%, renewables reaching over half of supply, gas about 20%, and nuclear about 10% by 2050. Regional energy mixes vary.

nodes.title: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: The outlook projects transportation energy demand to rise nearly 25% by 2050, with commercial fleets continuing to rely on liquid fuels while efficiency and electric vehicles reduce light-duty fuel use. Industrial and residential/commercial energy demand will grow, with oil remaining important as an industrial feedstock and electricity and natural gas gaining share. Liquid-fuels demand is forecast to reach nearly 115 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, increasingly concentrated in non-OECD countries and supplied by conventional crude and growing alternative sources; timely investment is essential. Natural-gas demand will rise nearly 20%, led by Asia Pacific, supported by unconventional gas, continued conventional production, and expanding LNG trade.

summary: Management oversees financial reporting for ExxonMobil’s integrated businesses and segments, supported by centralized services and a developing low-carbon business. Its planning processes establish economic assumptions and operating, investment, and emissions objectives; projects are assessed against long-term fundamentals and reviewed for lessons. The long-term Outlook, informed by multiple scenarios and monitored transition trends, guides planning and investment through 2050. It forecasts rising global energy demand, especially in developing countries, greater electricity use, changing generation mixes, and growth in transportation, industrial, and buildings demand. Liquid fuels remain important, while natural gas, renewables, nuclear, and alternative fuel sources expand; regional mixes differ, and timely investment is essential.

nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s 2025 Global Outlook projects a diverse energy mix through 2050: oil remains the largest source at nearly 30%, natural gas rises above 25%, coal’s share falls to about half of gas, nuclear grows, and renewables exceed 20%. Wind and solar increase nearly 350% from 2024 to exceed 10%, while other renewables contribute over 10%. Industrial decarbonization requires stable policies and a range of technologies, including lower-emission fuels, hydrogen and hydrogen-derived fuels, and carbon capture and storage (CCS). These solutions can support transport, including aviation and commercial vehicles, industrial heating, power generation, and heavy industries.

nodes.title: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: The discussion presents oil and gas supply-and-demand projections and their sources, including IEA, ExxonMobil, and IPCC scenarios. ExxonMobil expects oil demand to exceed 100 million barrels per day through 2050; even in likely-below-2°C scenarios, demand reaches 65 million. Without continued investment, oil production could decline roughly 15% annually, leaving a major 2030 shortfall; limiting production to existing fields slows decline but still fails to meet demand. Meeting demand, even under aggressive decarbonization, requires substantial investment, technology, and growth in resources from discoveries and existing fields. The Outlook accounts for evolving climate policies, uses assumed 2050 CO₂ proxy costs of up to $150 per metric ton in OECD and $100 elsewhere, and monitors Paris Agreement commitments and net-zero policies while emphasizing affordable, reliable energy. Projections draw on internal analyses and public sources.

nodes.title: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil describes its strategy for competitive, flexible growth and its ambition for net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions in operated assets by 2050, contingent on technology and supportive policy. It outlines 2030 intensity-reduction targets, progress exceeding several targets by year-end 2025, and investments in emissions reduction, including CCS, hydrogen, fuels, lithium, and other solutions. It summarizes 2025 oil, gas, refining, and chemical market conditions; tariff uncertainty; and $15.1 billion in structural savings toward a $20 billion 2030 goal. It also notes geopolitical risks to Kazakhstan oil exports through CPC and related earnings and production exposure.

title: BUSINESS RESULTS

Key Recent Events
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil describes an Upstream strategy focused on selective, low-cost growth, technology, efficient project delivery, and risk mitigation. Production reached a 40-year high of 4.7 million oil-equivalent barrels per day in 2025, with Americas, Permian, Guyana, and LNG expected to grow as shares of output. Future volumes and prices face operational, market, political, regulatory, and investment uncertainties. Recent developments include Guyana’s record production and planned FPSO expansions; Permian record output, a 2030 growth target, and 2035 net-zero goal; and LNG project progress in Papua New Guinea, Mozambique, and the United States. Upstream earnings were $21.4 billion in 2025; lower prices and base-volume declines reduced earnings, while advantaged growth, cost savings, other factors, and derivative timing supported them. Identified items included 2025 impairment losses and 2024 divestment-related effects.

nodes.title: Tax, Derivative, Fair Value, and Inventory Policies
nodes.summary: The Corporation excludes certain sales and value-added taxes collected as a government agent from revenue, reports other such taxes gross, and recognizes U.S. tax on global intangible low-taxed income as incurred. Derivatives may support trading or hedge commodity, currency, and interest-rate exposures; most are measured at fair value, with qualifying offsets and collateral netting. Non-hedge gains and losses enter earnings immediately; fair-value hedge changes enter earnings, while cash-flow hedge changes first enter other comprehensive income and later earnings. Fair value uses a three-level input hierarchy from active-market quoted prices to unobservable inputs. Crude oil, products, and merchandise are valued at the lower of market or cost, generally using LIFO; cost includes directly and indirectly incurred inventory-related charges but excludes selling and administrative expenses. Materials and supplies are valued at cost or less.

nodes.title: Property, Plant, and Equipment
nodes.summary: The Corporation follows the successful-efforts method, accumulating exploration and production costs by field. Property acquisition costs are capitalized; exploratory well costs are capitalized only when reserves and project viability justify completion, while other qualifying-failure well costs and geophysical costs and lease rentals are expensed. Development costs and qualifying multiyear construction-phase interest are capitalized, with interest depreciated over the related assets’ service lives. Depreciation, depletion, and amortization use unit-of-production or straight-line methods based on estimated service lives and obsolescence. Proved-property acquisition costs are amortized using total proved reserves; productive exploratory and development costs use proved developed reserves recoverable from existing facilities under current methods. Production is measured at custody-transfer or sales points.

nodes.title: NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
nodes.summary: The notes describe depreciation policies: unit-of-production is replaced by straight-line when it better reflects asset life; de-booked reserves may use updated SEC-price reserves, while refinery equipment and service-station improvements have 25- and 20-year lives. Repairs are expensed; major improvements are capitalized and replaced assets retired. Impairment reviews follow ASC 360/932 and consider market, operational, legal, cost, loss, and disposal indicators. Long-term prices, margins, development plans, and cash flows inform assessments; temporary downturns and standardized reserve cash-flow measures are not considered reliable impairment indicators on their own.

title: CODE OF ETHICS AND BUSINESS CONDUCT

nodes.title: Ethics and Conflicts of Interest
nodes.summary: The Company requires compliance with applicable laws and the highest standards of integrity, fairness, and honesty. Employees must accurately maintain books and records, cooperate candidly with auditors, follow policies and controls, and report material information to support full, fair, accurate, timely, and understandable regulatory and public disclosures. Directors, officers, and employees must avoid actual or apparent conflicts, including misusing corporate opportunities, trading on material nonpublic information, or competing with the Company.

nodes.title: Corporate Assets and Directorships Policies
nodes.summary: The Company expects directors, officers, and employees to protect and efficiently use its tangible and intangible assets, and forbids unauthorized use or disclosure of personal or confidential business information during or after service. Officers and employees face restrictions on nonaffiliated for-profit directorships, which must not conflict with or interfere with Company duties; nonprofit directorships are permitted unless they create such conflicts or obligate Company support. Affiliated-company service is allowed and may be a normal assignment. Directors’ public-company seats require Board approval; other nonaffiliated for-profit seats require management approval as directed by the Chairman.

nodes.title: Procedures and Open Door Communication
nodes.summary: Employees are encouraged to raise business questions, concerns, and suggestions and promptly report suspected legal, policy, or internal-control violations, which management investigates; Internal Audit leads internal-control investigations, with objective judgment expected. Employees should first approach supervisors, escalate unresolved issues, or use relevant departments. Allegations involving directors or executives and accounting or auditing concerns go to the General Auditor and, as applicable, Board or Audit Committee. Employees may contact nonemployee directors or submit anonymous complaints through specified channels. Confidentiality is handled with discretion but may not be practicable. Good-faith reporting is protected; dishonesty or noncompliance may lead to discipline. Foundation policies cannot be waived; employees should seek guidance, and approved activities are deemed nonviolations, while violations prompt action.

key_items: Exxon Mobil Corporation Rule 10D-1 Recoupment Policy Effective December 1, 2023
nodes.summary: Effective December 1, 2023, the policy implements NYSE Rule 10D-1 alongside other available recovery remedies, preventing duplicate recovery. It requires prompt recovery of excess covered compensation received by covered executives during the recovery period after a financial restatement, disregarding taxes. The Committee reasonably estimates stock-price or shareholder-return effects and documents estimates for the NYSE. Recovery may be impracticable if documented enforcement costs exceed recovery or recovery threatens specified tax-qualified retirement-plan status. Recovery methods may include repayment, set-off, cancellation, or future compensation reductions. The Corporation will not insure, indemnify, or reimburse executives for losses; the Compensation Committee administers the policy, and its decisions are final and binding.
